1:
Both of the voices that date the psalm put it late, on different evidence. Adam Clarke notes it has no title, assigns it most probably to the times after the captivity, and applies it to the opposition that Sanballat, Geshem and Tobiah gave the Jews while they rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem. Keil and Delitzsch argue from the language: the circumstantial phrase used here for the upright in their hearts stands in place of an older and shorter form, and two other expressions are equally late, so that this is one of the latest psalms. Their reading of the situation is that the people are under foreign dominion, and that in this lies the seductive inducement to apostasy, the faithful and the apostate being already separated.

The comparison to the hills draws three of them into topography, each importing a different describer. John Gill quotes a Roman historian calling the city inaccessible, surrounded by walls and mountains, rocks and towers, and adds a Greek poet who mentions a people speaking the Phoenician tongue who inhabited the mountains of Solyma, a name found in Homer and, on the same historian’s authority, the origin of the city’s own. Clarke quotes a traveller who has the city on a rocky mountain, everywhere steep but a little on the north, set as if in the midst of an amphitheatre, with named valleys separating it from the hills on each side; and he concludes that the situation was such as to be easily rendered impregnable. Charles Ellicott quotes a modern surveyor to opposite effect, that all the surrounding hills are higher than the city itself, and names them east, south, west and north in turn. John Calvin is uninterested in the survey and interested in why it is offered at all: the mountains are exhibited as a mirror to those who cannot sufficiently apprehend the secret protection of God by faith, the prophet accommodating himself to the rudeness of men still detained by the dulness of the flesh. Gill alone turns the figure against itself, reporting a Jewish commentator’s observation that the mountains did not in fact hinder the enemy from taking the city, whence he concludes that the Lord is the greater security. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same conclusion without the objection, that round about Jerusalem are mountains but more important still is the God who encompasses his people. Ellicott notes that a prophet elsewhere likens the same protection to a wall rather than to a rampart of hills.

Which Jerusalem is meant is settled by Augustine of Hippo from the failure of the promise on its face. If the earthly city is understood, all who dwelt in it have been removed by wars and by its destruction, and one may now seek a Jew in Jerusalem and not find him; therefore another city is meant, for which we sigh in this pilgrimage. Those who dwelt in the earthly one were moved first in heart and afterwards by exile, and when they had fallen in heart they cast their King outside their walls, so that he in turn cast them out of his. Matthew Henry keeps to the condition instead: all that deal with God must deal upon trust, and the closer our expectations are confined to him the higher they may be raised. C.H. Spurgeon presses the promise’s scope, that the blessing comes not to some who trust but to all, and finds the image exact in the Hebrew, which says of the hill that it sits to eternity, neither bowing down nor moving to and fro.
3:
What the rod is and whose the lot are canvassed by John Gill, who offers the word first as a rod of correction in God’s hand, then as a sceptre and ensign of government, standing for the nations of the world or for the antichristian states, and notes a version that takes it for a tribe; the lot he reports being read either as the city or as the people who inherit the land. Charles Ellicott settles it without hesitation as the heathen sceptre, the righteous being those who hold fast to the religion of their fathers, and observes that the verb rendered rest is a word expressing the presence of tyranny. John Wesley gives the same in three words, their power and authority, and the lot as the habitations and persons of good men.

The English of the verse provokes Adam Clarke into the sharpest institutional attack in the chapter. The liturgical version in use in his own church rendered the line as though the rod of the ungodly never came into the lot of the righteous at all, and Clarke quotes an older writer demolishing it in two counts: it is not truth, since the rod of the wicked does come into the inheritance of the righteous, and that often; and it is not scripture, since the text says only that it shall not rest there, so that it may come and stay for a time but shall not be permitted to abide. Clarke adds that this is only one, and not the worst, of the many blemishes deforming that version, calls it wholly unworthy of regard and fit to be thrown aside in favour of the authorised one, complains that the people are confounded by the differences between the two, and asks directly why the learned prelates of his day do not take away so sore a stumbling-block.

Why the tyranny is bounded at all is answered four ways. Ellicott says God will not suffer it to last lest the righteous be seduced or forced into connivance with practices that religion and patriotism unite to condemn. Keil and Delitzsch make it a proportion rather than a limit: the duration of the calamity is exactly measured against the power of resistance of the righteous, whom God proves and purifies by it while graciously preserving them. Clarke puts the danger institutionally, that were the wicked to bear rule in the Lord’s vineyard religion would soon become extinct. Wesley and Matthew Henry put it personally, that men under pressure are driven to indirect courses to relieve themselves. On the petition that follows, Gill reports a Jewish commentator who allowed it to be read either as a prayer or as a prophecy. Henry keeps it a prayer and marks its wording: it does not ask good for those that are perfect, sinless and spotless, but for those that are sincere and honest, so that those who are as they should be shall be as they would be. Keil and Delitzsch relay a rabbinic riddle on the same verse, that a good one received a good thing from the good One for the good ones. On the last verse Gill and Keil and Delitzsch converge on the same class, not open profane sinners but professors who desert under persecution and are afraid to confess God. Henry marks a distinction of his own, that the psalmist does not pray for their ruin but predicts it, and observes that sinful ways are called crooked because sin is the perverting of what is right.
